The blue mussel Mytilus edulis exhibits a life-history trajectory shaped by the cold, productive waters of the North Atlantic. Upon fertilisation, successive cleavage divisions produce a blastula-stage embryo that develops into a free-swimming trochophore larva within a remarkably short interval. At a water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the time from ovum activation to the hatching event is approximately 0.2 days [ab = approximately 0.2 days], a rapid progression that reflects the species' opportunistic reproductive strategy. The newly emerged veliger larva initially carries a residual yolk supply, transitioning quickly to planktotrophic feeding through cilia-driven capture of phytoplankton. At the moment of eclosion, the prodissoconch shell height from umbo to ventral margin measures just 0.009 cm [Lb = 0.009 cm]. The corresponding wet weight at this earliest stage is minuscule, calculated at 0.0000000269 grams [Wwb = 0.0000000269 grams] based on the allometric relationship established by Hare and Kooy (1993). This extreme neonatal lightness enables efficient pelagic dispersal, a critical adaptation for colonising ephemeral substrates in the intertidal zone where adult beds often develop.

As the growing pediveliger approaches metamorphic competence, it begins to explore benthic substrates, eventually settling and undergoing the rapid morphological transformation that marks the transition to the post-metamorphic juvenile stage. The shell height at which sexual maturation becomes physiologically possible is approximately 1.2 cm [Lp = approximately 1.2 cm], a size that is typically attained roughly one year after settlement under favourable conditions. The corresponding wet weight at the onset of puberty is 0.0638 grams [Wwp = 0.0638 grams], a value similarly derived from published length-weight regressions. This moderate size at maturation places the blue mussel at an intermediate position among mytilids, balancing early reproductive output against the survival advantages of continued somatic growth. Under optimal thermal conditions of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the time since birth at puberty is approximately 365 days since birth [tp = approximately 365 days since birth], indicating a relatively fast life-history pace for a bivalve capable of reaching substantial adult dimensions. The onset of gametogenesis marks a clear shift in physiological priority, with energy increasingly diverted from tissue production to the development of gonadal material.

At a stable water temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) reached 20% [GSI = 20%] during peak spawning condition. This relatively high allocation is characteristic of a species that produces numerous small offspring and relies on high fecundity rather than parental care to sustain population turnover. Following the spring phytoplankton bloom, females release substantial numbers of eggs into the water column each day. Under the productive conditions typical of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the maximum reproductive rate is achieved through a combination of clutch size and spawning frequency; specifically, females produce approximately 2 million eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 2 million eggs per spawning event], and can undergo a single spawning event each day [F_R_i = single spawning event each day] over the brief peak of the bloom.

The species' ultimate size is constrained by both environmental factors and intrinsic physiological limits. The maximum recorded shell height from umbo to ventral margin reaches 15 cm [Li = 15 cm] in protected, nutrient-rich embayments where competition and predation are low. This size corresponds to an ultimate wet weight of 124.6 grams [Wwi = 124.6 grams], representing the largest individuals within a population that often experiences heavy fishing pressure and storm-induced mortality before reaching such dimensions. The attainment of this asymptotic size requires several years of uninterrupted growth; however, natural mortality in the intertidal zone is high, and the maximum lifespan for the species in the wild is recorded as approximately 8760 days [am = approximately 8760 days] when maintained at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This longevity of nearly 24 years is exceptional for a bivalve of this trophic level, and it allows individuals that escape early mortality to become dominant space holders on the seafloor, their larger shells providing complex microhabitat for a diverse assemblage of epibionts.

The interplay between temperature, food availability, and physiological condition drives significant intraspecific variation in growth and reproduction across the broad geographic range of Mytilus edulis. Populations at the southern edge of the species' distribution, where summer water temperatures regularly exceed 20 °C, often exhibit reduced adult body sizes; these mussels rarely surpass a shell height of 10 cm, an observation that contrasts with the 15 cm [Li = 15 cm] maxima recorded in cooler northern latitudes. Similarly, the gonado-somatic index can vary markedly between years, reflecting the interannual variability in spring phytoplankton blooms. The gonadosomatic index of 20% [GSI = 20%] at 12 °C [T = 12 °C] may decline to below 10% during years of poor food supply. This physiological plasticity underscores the blue mussel's capacity to buffer interannual environmental variability through flexible allocation decisions, a trait that has undoubtedly contributed to its success as a foundation species across the temperate and subarctic coastal zone.
